paper_topic: Data Repetition Beats Data Scaling in Long-CoT SFT: under a fixed update budget, more epochs on smaller SFT datasets outperforms more unique samples

nodes.text: Modern language model training proceeds through distinct stages: pretraining on internet-scale data to acquire world knowledge, mid-training on curated corpora to extend capabilities, and post-training to shape model behavior (Guo et al., 2025; Team OLMo, 2025; Yang et al., 2025).
nodes.display_label: LM training stages: pretrain → mid → post

nodes.text: For reasoning-focused models, post-training typically begins with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) demonstrations, often distilled from more capable models, where reasoning traces can span thousands of tokens before reaching a final answer.

This SFT step, analogous to behavioral cloning in reinforcement learning (Osa et al., 2018), primes the model for subsequent stages such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (Ouyang et al., 2022) or reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (Guo et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024).
nodes.display_label: SFT primes for downstream RL stages

nodes.text: Unlike pretraining data, which can be scraped at scale from the web, high-quality long-CoT demonstrations require either expensive human annotation or careful distillation from larger models, including generation, filtering, and validation of long reasoning traces.
nodes.display_label: long-CoT data is expensive to obtain

nodes.text: As a result, the question of how to best utilize limited SFT data is practically important.
nodes.display_label: how to best use limited SFT data matters

nodes.text: The common assumption in machine learning would suggest that training with more unique training samples yields better generalization.
nodes.display_label: common assumption: more unique samples is better

nodes.text: Under i.i.d. sampling, each new example provides independent information about the data distribution, and generalization bounds in statistical learning theory typically improve with dataset size.
nodes.display_label: theory: generalization bounds improve with size

nodes.text: This principle manifests practically throughout the field – data augmentation techniques are widely used to artificially expand effective dataset size when real data is limited (Hernández-García & König, 2018; Shorten & Khoshgoftaar, 2019), and the success of large language models has been attributed in significant part to training on ever-larger unique corpora.
Following this logic, modern post-training pipelines employ millions of SFT samples (Team OLMo, 2025).
nodes.display_label: pipelines use millions of SFT samples

nodes.text: In this paper, we show that this might not only be suboptimal,
but that, actually, a reverse pattern can be observed for the SFT stage for a pretrained LLM, see Figure 1.
nodes.display_label: reverse pattern observed at SFT stage (Fig. 1)

nodes.text: Under a fixed update budget, training for more epochs on smaller datasets outperforms training on larger datasets.
nodes.display_label: more epochs on smaller data wins under fixed budget

nodes.text: The gains are not marginal.

The performance and termination rates, i.e., the model’s ability to successfully conclude reasoning with a final answer, both scale with epoch count and saturate together, suggesting that sufficient repetition of the same data is required for models to fully internalize the demonstrated reasoning structure.
nodes.display_label: perf + termination rate co-scale with epochs

nodes.text: We find that this convergence is tightly linked to training set memorization.
Performance improvements plateau once models achieve near-perfect next-token prediction accuracy on the training data, even as validation loss continues to rise.
This relationship holds across all models we test, all benchmarks, and different training datasets, making train token accuracy a practical stopping criterion for scaling epochs.
Despite this apparent overfitting, we observe no additional catastrophic forgetting compared to single-epoch training on large datasets.
We demonstrate that under a fixed update budget, scaling epochs on smaller datasets substantially outperforms scaling unique samples.

We identify training token accuracy as a reliable stopping criterion for epoch scaling, with performance gains plateauing once models reach full memorization, and we show that multi-epoch training on small datasets causes no additional catastrophic forgetting compared to large datasets.
We show how training data properties, such as teacher model size in distillation and the correctness of data samples, affect the repetition advantage.
While we provide a practical heuristic for exploiting the repetition advantage, we pose explaining this phenomenon in long-CoT SFT as a novel, open problem for the community.

observations:
FA0022 (Data Repetition Beats Data Scaling) follows a Context → Prior_Work → (single) Limitation → long Result chain → Contribution-bullets arc. The intro has an unusually long Context block (N1–N7) that builds up the field's worldview in two layers: practical motivation for SFT (N1–N5: training stages, long-CoT SFT, expense of CoT data) and the theoretical assumption underpinning data scaling (N6–N7: more unique samples = better generalization).

The Prior_Work block (N8–N9) crystallizes how the field operationalizes that assumption: data augmentation + ever-larger corpora (N8) and modern pipelines using millions of SFT samples (N9). The paper's thesis sentence is split N10a/N10b along its internal contrast ("not only suboptimal, but actually a reverse pattern"): N10a is the Limitation critique of N9's practice, N10b is the empirical Result. The Result chain is the longest segment (N10b–N17), covering the headline finding (more epochs on smaller data wins), supporting findings (gains not marginal, perf+termination co-scale, link to memorization, train-token-acc as stopping criterion, no extra catastrophic forgetting).

The Contribution block is a 3-bullet enumeration (N18a Phenomenon, N18b Dynamics, N18c Factors) directly summarizing the Result chain, with a meta-Contribution closing line (N19) framing the explanation as an open problem. N17 forks into the three contribution bullets, making it a fork node by topology. N18a carries an addresses edge back to N10a (both share the distinctive "scaling epochs / samples / suboptimal" lexical hook — N18a explicitly says "scaling epochs on smaller datasets substantially outperforms scaling unique samples", which directly resolves the Limitation that the millions-of-samples practice may be suboptimal).

Notable: no anchor paper — the target of critique is a field-wide practice (data scaling for SFT), not a single named system. The PDF intro is roughly 2.5× longer than the previously OCR-truncated markdown (which cut off mid-sentence at N3 and dropped most of the Result chain and the entire 3-bullet Contribution block). The contrast on N10a→N10b is carried by a real "but" marker (the marker test passes); the elaboration on N9→N10a reflects that the marker before "In this paper, we show" is the soft "In this paper" which is not in the canonical contrast list.
